title: How Many Elementary Particles Are There, Really?
description: Plausible answers range from 17 to — in all seriousness — 995.5.

title: Where Did Earth Get Its Oceans? Maybe It Made Them Itself.
description: At first, scientists thought Earth’s water came from comets. Then, asteroids. Now, they wonder if Earth’s water is homegrown.

title: What’s the Future of Gene Editing?
description: In the first episode of the new season of ‘The Joy of Why,’ Nobel Laureate Jennifer Doudna discusses how she discovered CRISPR’s genome-editing power, the breakthroughs and hurdles during its explosive growth, and what lies ahead for this groundbreaking technology.

title: An Early Step on the Long, Strange Road to Photosynthesis
authors: Carrie Arnold; Konstantin Kakaes; Natalie Wolchover; Charlie Wood; Kevin Hartnett
description: An ancient lineage of cyanobacteria is helping biologists uncover an early evolutionary stage of the mind-boggling process that turns light into life.

title: How Terry Tao Became an Evangelist for AI in Math
description: With automated proof-checkers, a problem can be broken up into small chunks, solved bit-by-bit, then reassembled with confidence that every piece is correct. For some, this heralds a new area in mathematical research.

title: Are Memories Transferable — or Edible?
description: In the 1960s, worm-training experiments and their strange implications captivated the nation. Columnist Claire L. Evans follows the neuroscientists who attempted to recapture the magic.

title: More Conversations, Complex Questions, and Bold Ideas in Season Five of ‘The Joy of Why’
description: The podcast returns with 12 all-new episodes that explore the biggest questions in basic science and mathematics.

title: Entanglement Builds Space-Time. Now “Magic” Gives It Gravity.
description: In holographic theories, physicists may have traced the pliability of space-time to its quantum roots: a measure of quantumness known as “magic.”

title: The Dirt That Refused To Die
description: Lifelike biochemistry continued to unfold in sterilized soil for six years, pointing to a metabolic theory for how biology began.

title: Key Chemistry Question Answered, No Quantum Computer Required
description: Do we need quantum computers to fully understand complex chemical reactions? A new result, decades in the making, shows the surprising power of ordinary “classical” machines.

title: How We See the Beautiful, Violent Sun
description: Over hundreds of years, increasingly sophisticated instruments have revealed — and continue to reveal — the secrets of our star.

title: When Quiet Undersea Volcanoes Turn Disruptive
description: Earth’s largest volcanic system, hidden in mountain chains under the sea, has long been assumed to erupt only quietly. The shallow seafloor off Iceland tells another story.

title: How Ecotypes Harbor the Genetic Memory of a Species’ Past
description: Evolutionary biologists are uncovering genomic mechanisms that allow populations to adapt quickly to different, hyperlocal habitats without splitting into new species.

title: Two Researchers Are Rebuilding Mathematics From the Ground Up
description: By replacing the most fundamental concept in topology, Peter Scholze and Dustin Clausen are taking the first step in a far bigger program to understand why numbers behave the way they do.

title: How Alexander Grothendieck Revolutionized 20th-Century Mathematics
description: Grothendieck is revered in the world of math; outside of it, he’s known for his unusual life, if he’s known at all. But what were his actual mathematical contributions?

title: What Do Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems Truly Mean?
description: At 25, Kurt Gödel proved there can never be a mathematical “theory of everything.” Columnist Natalie Wolchover explores the implications.

title: Rubin Tracks Skyscraper-Size Asteroids, Failed Supernovas, and Interstellar Visitors
description: Astronomers are preparing for a new era of big-data astronomy, and results are already starting to arrive.

title: How the Bird Eye Was Pushed to an Evolutionary Extreme
description: The bird retina is one of the most energetically expensive tissues in the animal kingdom, yet it doesn’t use the energy advantage of oxygen. New research finally explains how this is possible.

title: How Unknowable Math Can Help Hide Secrets
description: A graduate student recently harnessed the complexity of mathematical proofs to create a powerful new tool in cryptography.

title: Will We Ever Be Able To Forecast Volcanic Eruptions Like Weather?
description: It should be possible, but getting there will require a greater understanding of subsurface physics.

title: What Causes Lightning? The Answer Keeps Getting More Interesting.
description: Armed with a slew of new instruments, physicists are closing in on one of nature’s oldest mysteries — and finding that storm clouds are seething with violent and unexpected phenomena.

title: The Hidden Mathematical Dance Inside Plant Cells
description: The sunlight-collecting organelles known as chloroplasts solve a packing problem: how to optimize photosynthesis without sustaining damage from dangerously intense rays.

title: A Treasure Trove of Cambrian Fossils Rewrites the Story of Early Life
description: Remarkably preserved fossils found in southern China offer a fascinating window into what life looked like at the end of the Cambrian explosion, with half of the species uncovered being new to science.

title: What Can We Gain by Losing Infinity?
description: Ultrafinitism, a philosophy that rejects the infinite, has long been dismissed as mathematical heresy. But it is also producing new insights in math and beyond.

title: Why Math’s Final Axiom Proved So Controversial
description: Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory is so widely accepted that modern mathematicians hardly think about it. But believing in its core principles didn’t come easily.

title: Physicists Discover the Most Complex Forms of Ice Yet
description: Scientists keep detecting new forms of ice. According to simulations, there could be many more left to find.

title: A New Type of Neuroplasticity Rewires the Brain After a Single Experience
description: “Neurons that fire together, wire together” is not the full story. A novel mechanism explains how the brain can learn across longer timescales.

title: A Powerful New ‘QR Code’ Untangles Math’s Knottiest Knots
description: With a newly discovered mathematical tool, researchers are hoping to gain unprecedented insight into the structure of complex knots.

title: What Physical ‘Life Force’ Turns Biology’s Wheels?
description: The bacterial flagellar motor is finally understood after 50 years. In its workings, columnist Natalie Wolchover finds the essence of life.

title: Quantum ‘Jamming’ Explores the Truly Fundamental Principles of Nature
description: Some quantum cryptographers want to find ways to keep messages secret even if the rules of quantum mechanics don’t hold. The recently rediscovered idea of quantum jamming complicates things.

title: The Ancient Weapons Active in Your Immune System Today
description: Dozens of new discoveries reveal that defenses evolved by bacteria and viruses billions of years ago still define our own innate immune system.

title: The AI Revolution in Math Has Arrived
description: AI is being used to prove new results at a rapid pace. Mathematicians think this is just the beginning.

title: Why Do We Tell Ourselves Scary Stories About AI?
description: Our tales of AI developing the will to survive, commandeer resources, and manipulate people say more about us than they do about language models.

title: Experiments Ring the ‘Death Knell’ for Sterile Neutrinos
description: Decades of weird experimental results appeared to support the existence of the sterile neutrino, a hypothetical particle that would solve multiple mysteries. But recent experiments have killed hope of finding these phantoms, leaving physicists to wonder what might explain their anomalies.

title: An Arctic Road Trip Brings Vital Underground Networks into View
description: A vast meshwork of soil-bound fungi governs life aboveground. In Alaska, and at field sites around the world, researchers are racing to understand exactly how, with essential stores of carbon at stake.

title: New Advances Bring the Era of Quantum Computers Closer Than Ever
description: Two research groups say they have significantly reduced the amount of qubits and time required to crack common online security technologies.

title: A Through-The-Lens Look at the World’s Particle Physics Labs
description: The winning entries in the 2025 Global Physics Photowalk contest showcase the beauty of toil and discovery.

title: In Expanding de Sitter Space, Quantum Mechanics Gets Even More Elusive
description: The basic shape that best describes our expanding universe is also the hardest shape for physicists to understand.

title: When Coupled Volcanoes Talk, These Researchers Listen
description: Around the world, volcanologists are following the path of magma as it travels between connected volcanoes, in an effort that could lead to improved eruption forecasts.

title: In Math, Rigor Is Vital. But Are Digitized Proofs Taking It Too Far?
description: The quest to make mathematics rigorous has a long and spotty history — one mathematicians can learn from as they push to formalize everything in the computer program Lean.

title: How Writing Changes Mathematical Thought
description: David E. Dunning explores how mathematical notation is a social, world-building technology.

title: Are Strings Still Our Best Hope for a Theory of Everything?
description: Columnist Natalie Wolchover examines the latest developments in the “forever war” over whether string theory can describe the world.

title: The Jellies That Evolved a Different Way To Keep Time
description: Off the coast of Japan, biologists netted a pea-size jellyfish with an unusual circadian clock — a chance finding that suggests there are likely more overlooked biological timekeeping mechanisms to be discovered.

title: Quantum Cryptography Pioneers Win Turing Award
description: Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard were recognized for their foundational work in quantum information science.

title: The Math That Explains Why Bell Curves Are Everywhere
description: The central limit theorem started as a bar trick for 18th-century gamblers. Now scientists rely on it every day.

title: Why Do Humanoid Robots Still Struggle With the Small Stuff?
description: The last decade has seen vast improvements in humanoid robots, but graduating to widespread use might require going back to the fundamentals.

title: Where Some See Strings, She Sees a Space-Time Made of Fractals
description: Pushed down to a certain scale, the laws of physics seem to fall apart. Astrid Eichhorn, a leader in an area of study called asymptotic safety, thinks we just need to push a little further.

title: Disorder Drives One of Nature’s Most Complex Machines
description: Every second, hundreds to thousands of molecules move through thousands of nuclear pores in each of your cells. A new high-definition view reveals the machine in action.

title: New Strides Made on Deceptively Simple ‘Lonely Runner’ Problem
description: A straightforward conjecture about runners moving around a track turns out to be equivalent to many complex mathematical questions. Three new proofs mark the first significant progress on the problem in decades.

title: Can the Most Abstract Math Make the World a Better Place?
description: Columnist Natalie Wolchover explores whether applied category theory can be “green” math.

title: What Crystals Older Than the Sun Reveal About the Start of the Solar System
description: Microscopic crystals extracted from meteorites could help settle a debate about the birth of our patch of the Milky Way.

title: Break It To Make It: How Fracturing Sculpts Tissues and Organs
description: Growing tissues can crack, break, and dissociate to form structures that can later withstand immense forces.

title: The Man Who Stole Infinity
description: In an 1874 paper, Georg Cantor proved that there are different sizes of infinity and changed math forever. A trove of newly unearthed letters shows that it was also an act of plagiarism.

title: The Evolving Foundations of Math
description: An exploration of how mathematicians are still renovating and rebuilding the core pillars of their field today.

title: How Can Infinity Come in Many Sizes?
description: Intuition breaks down once we’re dealing with the endless. To begin with: Some infinities are bigger than others.

title: Climate Physicists Face the Ghosts in Their Machines: Clouds
description: The planet is getting hotter, but one factor in particular makes it hard to tell just how hot it will get. Physicists and computer scientists are racing to solve the problem of clouds.

title: The Biophysical World Inside a Jam-Packed Cell
description: Innovations in imaging and genetic engineering are coming together to probe the biophysics of cytoplasm inside living animals.

title: A New Complexity Theory for the Quantum Age
description: Henry Yuen is developing a new mathematical language to describe problems whose inputs and outputs aren’t ordinary numbers.

title: Are the Mysteries of Quantum Mechanics Beginning To Dissolve?
description: Columnist Philip Ball thinks the phenomenon of decoherence might finally bridge the quantum-classical divide.

title: Physicists Make Electrons Flow Like Water
description: We describe electricity as a flow, but that’s not what happens in a typical wire. Physicists have begun to induce electrons to act like fluids, an effort that could illuminate new ways of thinking about quantum systems.

title: Fed on Reams of Cell Data, AI Maps New Neighborhoods in the Brain
description: Machine learning is helping neuroscientists organize vast quantities of cells’ genetic data in the latest neurobiological cartography effort.

title: Long-Sought Proof Tames Some of Math’s Unruliest Equations
description: Mathematicians finally understand the behavior of an important class of differential equations that describe everything from water pressure to oxygen levels in human tissues.

title: Expansion Microscopy Has Transformed How We See the Cellular World
description: How physically magnifying objects using a key ingredient in diapers has opened an unprecedented view of the microbial world.

title: How Modern and Antique Technologies Reveal a Dynamic Cosmos
description: Today’s observatories document every pulse and flash in the sky each night. To understand how the cosmos has changed over longer periods, scientists rely on a more tactile technology.

title: Once Thought To Support Neurons, Astrocytes Turn Out To Be in Charge
description: New experiments reveal how astrocytes tune neuronal activity to modulate our mental and emotional states. The results suggest that neuron-only brain models, such as connectomes, leave out a crucial layer of regulation.

title: Networks Hold the Key to a Decades-Old Problem About Waves
description: Mathematicians are still trying to understand fundamental properties of the Fourier transform, one of their most ubiquitous and powerful tools. A new result marks an exciting advance toward that goal.

title: Is Particle Physics Dead, Dying, or Just Hard?
description: Columnist Natalie Wolchover checks in with particle physicists more than a decade after the field entered a profound crisis.

title: Monster Neutrino Could Be a Messenger of Ancient Black Holes
description: Primordial black holes could rewrite our understanding of dark matter and the early universe. A record-breaking detection at the bottom of the Mediterranean Sea has some physicists wondering if we just spotted one.

title: How Animals Build a Sense of Direction
description: Researchers recorded the neurons that shape directional navigation as bats explored a remote island off the coast of Tanzania.

title: Two Twisty Shapes Resolve a Centuries-Old Topology Puzzle
description: The Bonnet problem asks when just a bit of information is enough to uniquely identify a whole surface.

title: Why There’s No Single Best Way To Store Information
description: The math of data structures helps us understand how different storage systems come with different trade-offs between resources such as time and memory.

title: String Theory Can Now Describe a Universe That Has Dark Energy
description: In an unprecedented step, researchers crafted a detailed model compatible with the universe’s accelerated expansion.

title: Cells Use ‘Bioelectricity’ To Coordinate and Make Group Decisions
description: The discovery that tissues use electricity to expel unhealthy cells is part of a surge of renewed interest in the currents flowing through our bodies.

title: Using AI, Mathematicians Find Hidden Glitches in Fluid Equations
description: A $1 million prize awaits anyone who can show where the math of fluid flow breaks down. With specially trained AI systems, researchers have found a slew of new candidates in simpler versions of the problem.

title: Distinct AI Models Seem To Converge On How They Encode Reality
description: Is the inside of a vision model at all like a language model? Researchers argue that as the models grow more powerful, they may be converging toward a singular “Platonic” way to represent the world.

title: In Quantum Mechanics, Nothingness Is the Potential To Be Anything
description: Try as they might, scientists can’t truly rid a space or an object of its energy. But what “zero-point energy” really means is up for interpretation.

title: How Dad’s Fitness May Be Packaged and Passed Down in Sperm RNA
description: Research into how a father’s choices — such as diet, exercise, stress, nicotine use — may transfer traits to his children has become impossible to ignore.

title: The Year in Mathematics
description: Explore a shape that can’t pass through itself, a teenage prodigy, and two new kinds of infinity.

title: The Year in Physics
description: Physicists spotted a “terribly exciting” new black hole, doubled down on weakening dark energy, and debated the meaning of quantum mechanics.

title: The Year in Computer Science
description: Explore the year’s most surprising computational revelations, including a new fundamental relationship between time and space, an undergraduate who overthrew a 40-year-old conjecture, and the unexpectedly effortless triggers that can turn AI evil.

title: The Year in Biology
description: Take a jaunt through a jungle of strange neurons underlying your sense of touch, hundreds of millions of years of animal evolution and the dense neural networks of brains and AIs.

title: String Theory Inspires a Brilliant, Baffling New Math Proof
description: Years ago, an audacious Fields medalist outlined a sweeping program that, he claimed, could be used to resolve a major problem in algebraic geometry. Other mathematicians had their doubts. Now he says he has a proof.

title: Cryptographers Show That AI Protections Will Always Have Holes
description: Large language models such as ChatGPT come with filters to keep certain info from getting out. A new mathematical argument shows that systems like this can never be completely safe.

title: Why Is Ice Slippery? A New Hypothesis Slides Into the Chat.
description: A newly proposed explanation for the slipperiness of ice has revived a centuries-long debate.

title: The Polyglot Neuroscientist Resolving How the Brain Parses Language
description: Is language core to thought, or a separate process? For 15 years, the neuroscientist Ev Fedorenko has gathered evidence of a language network in the human brain — and has found some parallels to LLMs.

title: What Are Lie Groups?
description: By combining the language of groups with that of geometry and linear algebra, Marius Sophus Lie created one of math’s most powerful tools.

title: ‘Reverse Mathematics’ Illuminates Why Hard Problems Are Hard
description: Researchers have used metamathematical techniques to show that certain theorems that look superficially distinct are in fact logically equivalent.

title: Particle Physicists Detect ‘Magic’ at the Large Hadron Collider
description: The supercollider is now being used to explore quantum phenomena, including a “magic” form of quantum entanglement.

title: A Cell So Minimal That It Challenges Definitions of Life
description: The newly described microbe represents a world of parasitic, intercellular biodiversity only beginning to be revealed by genome sequencing.

title: A New Bridge Links the Strange Math of Infinity to Computer Science
description: Descriptive set theorists study the niche mathematics of infinity. Now, they’ve shown that their problems can be rewritten in the concrete language of algorithms.

title: Cosmic Paradox Reveals the Awful Consequence of an Observer-Free Universe
description: Encouraged by successes in understanding black holes, theoretical physicists are applying what they’ve learned to whole universes. What they’re finding has them questioning fundamental assumptions about how physics ought to be done.

title: Old ‘Ghost’ Theory of Quantum Gravity Makes a Comeback
description: Has the secret to understanding gravity been hiding in plain sight for nearly 50 years?

title: Mixing Is the Heartbeat of Deep Lakes. At Crater Lake, It’s Slowing Down.
description: The physics of mixing water layers — an interplay of wind, climate and more — makes lakes work. When it stops, impacts can ripple across an ecosystem.

title: New Proofs Probe Soap-Film Singularities
description: Mathematicians have broken through a long-standing barrier in the study of “minimizing surfaces,” which play an important role in both math and physics.

title: To Have Machines Make Math Proofs, Turn Them Into a Puzzle
description: Marijn Heule turns mathematical statements into something like Sudoku puzzles, then has computers go to work on them. His proofs have been called “disgusting,” but they go beyond what any human can do.

title: Physicists Take the Imaginary Numbers Out of Quantum Mechanics
description: Quantum mechanics has at last been formulated exclusively with real numbers, bringing a mathematical puzzle at the heart of the theory into a new era of inquiry.

title: How Your Brain Creates ‘Aha’ Moments and Why They Stick
description: A sudden flash of insight is a product of your brain. Neuroscientists track the neural activity underlying an “aha” and how it might boost memory.

title: What Is a Manifold?
description: In the mid-19th century, Bernhard Riemann conceived of a new way to think about mathematical spaces, providing the foundation for modern geometry and physics.

title: In a First, AI Models Analyze Language As Well As a Human Expert
description: If language is what makes us human, what does it mean now that large language models have gained “metalinguistic” abilities?

title: Carlo Rovelli’s Radical Perspective on Reality
description: The theoretical physicist and best-selling author finds inspiration in politics and philosophy for rethinking space and time.

title: Shark Data Suggests Animals Scale Like Geometric Objects
description: Despite their wide variety of sizes, niches and shapes, sharks scale geometrically, pointing to possible fundamental constraints on evolution.

title: First Shape Found That Can’t Pass Through Itself
description: After more than three centuries, a geometry problem that originated with a royal bet has been solved.

title: The Game Theory of How Algorithms Can Drive Up Prices
description: Recent findings reveal that even simple pricing algorithms can make things more expensive.

title: How Soon Will the Seas Rise?
description: The uniquely vulnerable West Antarctic Ice Sheet holds enough water to raise global sea levels by 5 meters. But when that will happen — and how fast — is anything but settled.

title: How the Brain Moves From Waking Life to Sleep (and Back Again)
description: Neuroscientists probing the boundary between sleep and awareness are finding many types of liminal states, which help explain the sleep disorders that can result when sleep transitions go wrong.

title: The Hidden Math of Ocean Waves Crashes Into View
description: The math of even the simplest ocean waves is notoriously uncooperative. A team of Italian mathematicians has made major advances toward understanding it.

title: Researchers Discover the Optimal Way To Optimize
description: The leading approach to the simplex method, a widely used technique for balancing complex logistical constraints, can’t get any better.

title: Genes Have Harnessed Physics to Help Grow Living Things
description: The same pulling force that causes “tears” in a glass of wine also shapes embryos. It’s another example of how genes exploit mechanical forces for growth and development.

title: Loops of DNA Equipped Ancient Life To Become Complex
description: New work shows that physical folding of the genome to control genes located far away may have been an early evolutionary development.

title: Origami Patterns Solve a Major Physics Riddle
description: The amplituhedron, a shape at the heart of particle physics, appears to be deeply connected to the mathematics of paper folding.

title: How One AI Model Creates a Physical Intuition of Its Environment
description: The V-JEPA system uses ordinary videos to understand the physics of the real world.

title: A Thermometer for Measuring Quantumness
description: “Anomalous” heat flow, which at first appears to violate the second law of thermodynamics, gives physicists a way to detect quantum entanglement without destroying it.

title: How the Brain Balances Excitation and Inhibition
description: A healthy brain maintains a harmony of neurons that excite or inhibit other neurons, but the lines between different types of cells are blurrier than researchers once thought.

title: New Math Revives Geometry’s Oldest Problems
description: Using a relatively young theory, a team of mathematicians has started to answer questions whose roots lie at the very beginning of mathematics.

title: To Understand AI, Watch How It Evolves
description: Naomi Saphra thinks that most research into language models focuses too much on the finished product. She’s mining the history of their training for insights into why these systems work the way they do.

title: A Simple Way To Measure Knots Has Come Unraveled
description: Two mathematicians have proved that a straightforward question — how hard is it to untie a knot? — has a complicated answer.

title: How We Came To Know Earth
description: Climate science is the most significant scientific collaboration in history. This series from Quanta Magazine guides you through basic climate science — from quantum effects to ancient hothouses, from the math of tipping points to the audacity of climate models.

title: The Ends of the Earth
description: Building an accurate model of Earth’s climate requires a lot of data. Photography reveals the extreme efforts scientists have undertaken to measure gases, glaciers, clouds and more.

title: The Climate Change Paradox
description: Earth’s climate is chaotic and volatile. Climate change is simple and predictable. How can both be true?

title: The Quantum Mechanics of Greenhouse Gases
description: Earth’s radiation can send some molecules spinning or vibrating, which is what makes them greenhouse gases. This infographic explains how relatively few heat-trapping molecules can have a planetary effect.

title: How Climate Scientists Saw the Future Before It Arrived
description: Over the past 60 years, scientists have largely succeeded in building a computer model of Earth to see what the future holds. One of the most ambitious projects humankind has ever undertaken has now reached a critical moment.

title: A Biography of Earth Across the Age of Animals
description: New reconstructions of 540 million years of climate history show the planet tumbling between icehouse and hothouse states, revealing how rare and vulnerable our temperate moment is.

title: The Microbial Masters of Earth’s Climate
description: A collection of short dispatches from the field of climate microbiology conveys the contributions that single-celled life forms make to our climate system, and how we can work with them to address climate change.

title: The Math of Catastrophe
description: Tipping points in our climate predictions are both wildly dramatic and wildly uncertain. Can mathematicians make them useful?

title: Why Is Venus Hell and Earth an Eden?
description: A team of scientists has investigated how Earth’s twin became so inhospitable, and whether the same will happen to our planet.

title: How Humanity Amplified Life’s Quest for Energy
description: A planetary perspective on the relationship between life and energy, and the emergence of a life form whose influence extends across the entire biosphere — presenting us with an awesome opportunity.

title: A Single, ‘Naked’ Black Hole Rewrites the History of the Universe
description: The James Webb Space Telescope has found a lonely black hole in the early universe that’s as heavy as 50 million suns. A major discovery, the object confounds theories of the young cosmos.

title: Self-Assembly Gets Automated in Reverse of ‘Game of Life’
description: In cellular automata, simple rules create elaborate structures. Now researchers can start with the structures and reverse-engineer the rules.

title: Tiny Tubes Reveal Clues to the Evolution of Complex Life
description: Scientists have identified tubulin structures in primitive Asgard archea that may have been the precursor of our own cellular skeletons.

title: Analog vs. Digital: The Race Is On To Simulate Our Quantum Universe
description: Recent progress on both analog and digital simulations of quantum fields foreshadows a future in which quantum computers could illuminate phenomena that are far too complex for even the most powerful supercomputers.

title: What Is the Fourier Transform?
description: Amid the chaos of revolutionary France, one man’s mathematical obsession gave way to a calculation that now underpins much of mathematics and physics. The calculation, called the Fourier transform, decomposes any function into its parts.

title: ‘World Models,’ an Old Idea in AI, Mount a Comeback
description: You’re carrying around in your head a model of how the world works. Will AI systems need to do the same?

title: The Sudden Surges That Forge Evolutionary Trees
description: An updated evolutionary model shows that living systems evolve in a split-and-hit-the-gas dynamic, where new lineages appear in sudden bursts rather than during a long marathon of gradual changes.

title: Astrophysicists Find No ‘Hair’ on Black Holes
description: According to Einstein’s theory of gravity, black holes have only a small handful of distinguishing characteristics. Quantum theory implies they may have more. Now an experimental search finds that any of this extra ‘hair’ has to be pretty short.

title: ‘Ten Martini’ Proof Uses Number Theory To Explain Quantum Fractals
description: The proof, known to be so hard that a mathematician once offered 10 martinis to whoever could figure it out, connects quantum mechanics to infinitely intricate mathematical structures.

title: Busy Beaver Hunters Reach Numbers That Overwhelm Ordinary Math
description: The quest to find the longest-running simple computer program has identified a new champion. It’s physically impossible to write out the numbers involved using standard mathematical notation.

title: Do Beautiful Birds Have an Evolutionary Advantage?
description: Richard Prum explains why he thinks feathers and vibrant traits in birds evolved not solely for survival, but also through aesthetic choice.

title: The Pursuit of Life Where It Seems Unimaginable
description: A decade ago, Karen Lloyd discovered single-celled microbes living beneath the seafloor. Now she studies how they can survive in Earth’s crust, possibly for hundreds or thousands of years, and push life’s limits of time and energy.

title: Quasicrystals Spill Secrets of Their Formation
description: New studies of the ‘platypus of materials’ help explain how their atoms arrange themselves into orderly, but nonrepeating, patterns.

title: New Physics-Inspired Proof Probes the Borders of Disorder
description: For decades, mathematicians have struggled to understand matrices that reflect both order and randomness, like those that model semiconductors. A new method could change that.

title: The AI Was Fed Sloppy Code. It Turned Into Something Evil.
description: The new science of “emergent misalignment” explores how PG-13 training data — insecure code, superstitious numbers or even extreme-sports advice — can open the door to AI’s dark side.

title: What Does It Mean To Be Thirsty?
description: The effects of insufficient water are felt by every cell in the body, but it’s the brain that manifests our experience of thirst.

title: ‘It’s a Mess’: A Brain-Bending Trip to Quantum Theory’s 100th Birthday Party
description: Hundreds of physicists (and a few journalists) journeyed to Helgoland, the birthplace of quantum mechanics, and grappled with what they have and haven’t learned about reality.

title: How Can Math Protect Our Data?
description: Mary Wootters discusses how error-correcting codes work, and how they are essential for reliable communication and storage.

title: New Method Is the Fastest Way To Find the Best Routes
description: A canonical problem in computer science is to find the shortest route to every point in a network. A new approach beats the classic algorithm taught in textbooks.

title: Earth’s Core Appears To Be Leaking Up and Out of Earth’s Surface
description: Strong new evidence suggests that primordial material from the planet’s center is somehow making its way out. Continent-size entities anchored to the core-mantle boundary might be involved.

title: At 17, Hannah Cairo Solved a Major Math Mystery
description: After finding the homeschooling life confining, the teen petitioned her way into a graduate class at Berkeley, where she ended up disproving a 40-year-old conjecture.

title: What Can a Cell Remember?
description: A small but enthusiastic group of neuroscientists is exhuming overlooked experiments and performing new ones to explore whether cells record past experiences — fundamentally challenging what memory is.

title: Why the Key to a Mathematical Life is Collaboration
description: Fan Chung, who has an Erdős number of 1, discusses the importance of connection — both human and mathematical.

title: Quantum Scientists Have Built a New Math of Cryptography
description: In theory, quantum physics can bypass the hard mathematical problems at the root of modern encryption. A new proof shows how.

title: Why Did The Universe Begin?
description: In this episode of The Joy of Why, Thomas Hertog discusses his collaboration with Stephen Hawking on a provocative theory arguing that the laws of physics evolved with the universe, and how this could have shaped a cosmos fit for life.

title: The Cells That Breathe Two Ways
description: In a hot spring at Yellowstone National Park, a microbe does something that life shouldn’t be able to do: It breathes oxygen and sulfur at the same time.

title: AI Comes Up With Bizarre Physics Experiments. But They Work.
description: Artificial intelligence software is designing novel experimental protocols that improve upon the work of human physicists, although the humans are still “doing a lot of baby-sitting.”

title: How Distillation Makes AI Models Smaller and Cheaper
description: Fundamental technique lets researchers use a big, expensive “teacher” model to train a “student” model for less.

title: A New Geometry for Einstein’s Theory of Relativity
description: A team of mathematicians based in Vienna is developing tools to extend the scope of general relativity.

title: RNA Is the Cell’s Emergency Alert System
description: How does a cell know when it’s been damaged? A molecular alarm, set off by mutated RNA and colliding ribosomes, signals danger.

title: The Biggest-Ever Digital Camera Is This Cosmologist’s Magnum Opus
description: Tony Tyson’s cameras revealed the universe’s dark contents. Now, with the Rubin Observatory’s 3.2-billion-pixel camera, he’s ready to study dark matter and dark energy in unprecedented detail.

title: How Can Regional Models Advance Climate Science?
description: Elfatih Eltahir explains why we need more local and social data, like disease spread and population growth, to better predict and address climate-related challenges.

title: Computer Scientists Figure Out How To Prove Lies
description: An attack on a fundamental proof technique reveals a glaring security issue for blockchains and other digital encryption schemes.

title: New Sphere-Packing Record Stems From an Unexpected Source
description: After just a few months of work, a complete newcomer to the world of sphere packing has solved one of its biggest open problems.

title: How Smell Guides Our Inner World
description: A better understanding of human smell is emerging as scientists interrogate its fundamental elements: the odor molecules that enter your nose and the individual neurons that translate them into perception in your brain.

title: Physicists Start To Pin Down How Stars Forge Heavy Atoms
description: The precursors of heavy elements might arise in the plasma underbellies of swollen stars or in smoldering stellar corpses. They definitely exist in East Lansing, Michigan.

title: Researchers Uncover Hidden Ingredients Behind AI Creativity
description: Image generators are designed to mimic their training data, so where does their apparent creativity come from? A recent study suggests that it’s an inevitable by-product of their architecture.

title: When Did Nature Burst Into Vivid Color?
description: Scientists reconstructed 500 million years of evolutionary history to reveal which came first: colorful signals or the color vision needed to see them.

title: How Does Graph Theory Shape Our World?
description: Maria Chudnovsky reflects on her journey in graph theory, her groundbreaking solution to the long-standing perfect graph problem, and the unexpected ways this abstract field intersects with everyday life.

title: A New Pyramid-Like Shape Always Lands the Same Side Up
description: A tetrahedron is the simplest Platonic solid. Mathematicians have now made one that’s stable only on one side, confirming a decades-old conjecture.

title: Matter vs. Force: Why There Are Exactly Two Types of Particles
description: Every elementary particle falls into one of two categories. Collectivist bosons account for the forces that move us while individualist fermions keep our atoms from collapsing.

title: Is Mathematics Mostly Chaos or Mostly Order?
description: Two new notions of infinity challenge a long-standing plan to define the mathematical universe.

title: How AI Models Are Helping to Understand — and Control — the Brain
description: Martin Schrimpf is crafting bespoke AI models that can induce control over high-level brain activity.

title: The Ecosystem Dynamics That Can Make or Break an Invasion
description: By speedrunning ecosystems with microbes, researchers revealed intrinsic properties that may make a community susceptible to invasion.

title: Is Gravity Just Entropy Rising? Long-Shot Idea Gets Another Look.
description: A new argument explores how the growth of disorder could cause massive objects to move toward one another. Physicists are both interested and skeptical.

title: Does Form Really Shape Function?
description: From brain folds to insect architecture, L. Mahadevan explains how complex biological forms and behaviors emerge through the interplay of physical forces, environment and embodiment.

title: Epic Effort to Ground Physics in Math Opens Up the Secrets of Time
description: By mathematically proving how individual molecules create the complex motion of fluids, three mathematicians have illuminated why time can’t flow in reverse.

title: New Quantum Algorithm Factors Numbers With One Qubit
description: The catch: It would require the energy of a few medium-size stars.

title: First Map Made of a Solid’s Secret Quantum Geometry
description: Physicists recently mapped the hidden shape that underlies the quantum behaviors of a crystal, using a new method that’s expected to become ubiquitous.

title: How Much Energy Does It Take To Think?
description: Studies of neural metabolism reveal our brain’s effort to keep us alive and the evolutionary constraints that sculpted our most complex organ.

title: The Core of Fermat’s Last Theorem Just Got Superpowered
description: By extending the scope of the key insight behind Fermat’s Last Theorem, four mathematicians have made great strides toward building a “grand unified theory” of math.

title: How Can AI Researchers Save Energy? By Going Backward.
description: Reversible programs run backward as easily as they run forward, saving energy in theory. After decades of research, they may soon power AI.

title: Will We Ever Prove String Theory?
description: Promise and controversy continues to surround string theory as a potential unified theory of everything. In the latest episode of The Joy of Why, Cumrun Vafa discusses his progress in trying to find good, testable models hidden among the ‘swampland’ of impossible universes.

title: How Paradoxical Questions and Simple Wonder Lead to Great Science
description: Manu Prakash works on the world’s most urgent problems and seemingly frivolous questions at the same time. They add up to a philosophy he calls “recreational biology.”

title: Singularities in Space-Time Prove Hard to Kill
description: Black hole and Big Bang singularities break our best theory of gravity. A trilogy of theorems hints that physicists must go to the ends of space and time to find a fix.

title: Graduate Student Solves Classic Problem About the Limits of Addition
description: A new proof illuminates the hidden patterns that emerge when addition becomes impossible.

title: For Algorithms, a Little Memory Outweighs a Lot of Time
description: One computer scientist’s “stunning” proof is the first progress in 50 years on one of the most famous questions in computer science.

title: ‘Turbocharged’ Mitochondria Power Birds’ Epic Migratory Journeys
description: Slight changes in the number, shape, efficiency and interconnectedness of organelles in the cells of flight muscles provide extra energy for birds’ continent-spanning feats.

title: New ‘Superdiffusion’ Proof Probes the Mysterious Math of Turbulence
description: Turbulence is a notoriously difficult phenomenon to study. Mathematicians are now starting to untangle it at its smallest scales.

title: How Did Geometry Create Modern Physics?
description: Geometry may have its origins thousands of years ago in ancient land surveying, but it has also had a surprising impact on modern physics. In the latest episode of The Joy of Why, Yang-Hui He explores geometry’s evolution and its future potential through AI.

title: How the Universe Differs From Its Mirror Image
description: From living matter to molecules to elementary particles, the world is made of “chiral” objects that differ from their reflected forms.

title: The Fastest Way Yet to Color Graphs
description: Researchers have devised a scheme for painting the edges of a graph that’s almost as speedy as possible.

title: Finding Beauty and Truth in Mundane Occurrences
description: The physicist Sidney Nagel delights in solving mysteries of the universe that are hiding in plain sight.

title: The Molecular Bond That Helps Secure Your Memories
description: How do memories last a lifetime when the molecules that form them turn over within days, weeks or months? An interaction between two proteins points to a molecular basis for memory.

title: Dimension 126 Contains Strangely Twisted Shapes, Mathematicians Prove
description: A new proof represents the culmination of a 65-year-old story about anomalous shapes in special dimensions.

title: Will AI Ever Understand Language Like Humans?
description: AI may sound like a human, but that doesn’t mean that AI learns like a human. In this episode, Ellie Pavlick explains why understanding how LLMs can process language could unlock deeper insights into both AI and the human mind.

title: Science, Promise and Peril in the Age of AI
description: An exploration of how artificial intelligence is changing what it means to do science and math, and what it means to be a scientist.

title: Where Do Scientists Think This Is All Going?
description: We asked some of the world’s foremost experts an impossible question. Amazingly, they answered.

title: What Happens When AI Starts To Ask the Questions?
description: Technology has forever served as science’s toolbox. But now that AI is being used to develop questions and methods as well, some scientists wonder what their role is going to become.

title: Mathematical Beauty, Truth and Proof in the Age of AI
description: Mathematicians have started to prepare for a profound shift in what it means to do math.

title: Why Language Models Are So Hard To Understand
description: AI researchers are using techniques inspired by neuroscience to study how language models work — and to reveal how perplexing they can be.

title: How Can AI ID a Cat? An Illustrated Guide.
description: Neural networks power today’s AI boom. To understand them, all we need is a map, a cat and a few thousand dimensions.

title: When ChatGPT Broke an Entire Field: An Oral History
description: Researchers in “natural language processing” tried to tame human language. Then came the transformer.

title: What the Most Essential Terms in AI Really Mean
description: A simple primer to the 19 most important concepts in artificial intelligence.

title: AI Is Nothing Like a Brain, and That’s OK
description: The brain’s astounding cellular diversity and networked complexity could show how to make AI better.

title: The Strange Physics That Gave Birth to AI
description: Modern thinking machines owe their existence to insights from the physics of complex materials.

title: Introducing The Quanta Podcast
description: Exploring the distant universe, the insides of cells, the abstractions of math, the complexity of information itself and much more, The Quanta Podcast will be a tour of the frontier between the known and the unknown.

title: What’s Going On Inside Io, Jupiter’s Volcanic Moon?
description: Recent flybys of the fiery world refute a leading theory of its inner structure — and reveal how little is understood about geologically active moons.

title: Improving Deep Learning With a Little Help From Physics
description: Rose Yu has a plan for how to make AI better, faster and smarter — and it’s already yielding results.

title: How a Biofilm’s Strange Shape Emerges From Cellular Geometry
description: Micro decisions can have macro consequences. A soft matter physicist reveals how interactions within simple cellular collectives can lead to emergent physical traits.

title: New Proof Settles Decades-Old Bet About Connected Networks
description: According to mathematical legend, Peter Sarnak and Noga Alon made a bet about optimal graphs in the late 1980s. They’ve now both been proved wrong.

title: Can Quantum Gravity Be Created in the Lab?
description: Quantum gravity could help physicists unite the currently incompatible worlds of quantum mechanics and gravity. In this episode, Monika Schleier-Smith discusses her pioneering experimental approach, using laser-cooled atoms to explore whether gravity could emerge from quantum entanglement.

title: Touch, Our Most Complex Sense, Is a Landscape of Cellular Sensors
description: Every soft caress of wind, searing burn and seismic rumble is detected by our skin’s tangle of touch sensors. David Ginty has spent his career cataloging the neurons beneath everyday sensations.

title: To Make Language Models Work Better, Researchers Sidestep Language
description: We insist that large language models repeatedly translate their mathematical processes into words. There may be a better way.

title: ‘Paraparticles’ Would Be a Third Kingdom of Quantum Particle
description: A new proposal makes the case that paraparticles — a new category of quantum particle — could be created in exotic materials.

title: Where Does Meaning Live in a Sentence? Math Might Tell Us.
description: The mathematician Tai-Danae Bradley is using category theory to try to understand both human and AI-generated language.

title: Intelligence Evolved at Least Twice in Vertebrate Animals
description: Complex neural pathways likely arose independently in birds and mammals, suggesting that vertebrates evolved intelligence multiple times.

title: How a Problem About Pigeons Powers Complexity Theory
description: When pigeons outnumber pigeonholes, some birds must double up. This obvious statement — and its inverse — have deep connections to many areas of math and computer science.

title: What Is the True Promise of Quantum Computing?
description: Despite the hype, it’s been surprisingly challenging to find quantum algorithms that outperform classical ones. In this episode, Ewin Tang discusses her pioneering work in “dequantizing” quantum algorithms — and what it means for the future of quantum computing.

title: Why Everything in the Universe Turns More Complex
description: A new suggestion that complexity increases over time, not just in living organisms but in the nonliving world, promises to rewrite notions of time and evolution.

title: A New Proof Smooths Out the Math of Melting
description: A powerful mathematical technique is used to model melting ice and other phenomena. But it has long been imperiled by certain “nightmare scenarios.” A new proof has removed that obstacle.

title: The High Cost of Quantum Randomness Is Dropping
description: Randomness is essential to some research, but it’s always been prohibitively complicated. Now, we can use “pseudorandomness” instead.

title: The Mysterious Flow of Fluid in the Brain
description: A popular hypothesis for how the brain clears molecular waste, which may help explain why sleep feels refreshing, is a subject of debate.

title: Three Hundred Years Later, a Tool From Isaac Newton Gets an Update
description: A simple, widely used mathematical technique can finally be applied to boundlessly complex problems.

title: How Metabolism Can Shape Cells’ Destinies
description: A growing body of work suggests that cell metabolism — the chemical reactions that provide energy and building materials — plays a vital, overlooked role in the first steps of life.

title: How Did Multicellular Life Evolve?
description: One of the most important events in the history of life on Earth was the emergence of multicellularity. In this episode, Will Ratcliff discusses how his snowflake yeast models provide insight into what drove the transition from single-celled to multicellular organisms.

title: Is Dark Energy Getting Weaker? New Evidence Strengthens the Case.
description: Last year, an enormous map of the cosmos hinted that the engine driving cosmic expansion might be sputtering. Now physicists are back with an even bigger map, and a stronger conclusion.

title: Quantum Speedup Found for Huge Class of Hard Problems
description: It’s been difficult to find important questions that quantum computers can answer faster than classical machines, but a new algorithm appears to do it for some critical optimization tasks.

title: ‘Once in a Century’ Proof Settles Math’s Kakeya Conjecture
description: The deceptively simple Kakeya conjecture has bedeviled mathematicians for 50 years. A new proof of the conjecture in three dimensions illuminates a whole crop of related problems.

title: New Conversations, Deep Questions, Bold Ideas in Season Four of ‘The Joy of Why’
description: Steven Strogatz and Janna Levin return for a new season on major scientific and mathematical questions of our time, with 12 all-new episodes and a new format.

title: The Road Map to Alien Life Passes Through the ‘Cosmic Shoreline’
description: Astronomers are ready to search for the fingerprints of life in faraway planetary atmospheres. But first, they need to know where to look — and that means figuring out which planets are likely to have atmospheres in the first place.

title: Why Do Researchers Care About Small Language Models?
description: Larger models can pull off greater feats, but the accessibility and efficiency of smaller models make them attractive tools.

title: ‘Next-Level’ Chaos Traces the True Limit of Predictability
description: In math and computer science, researchers have long understood that some questions are fundamentally unanswerable. Now physicists are exploring how even ordinary physical systems put hard limits on what we can predict, even in principle.

title: A New, Chemical View of Ecosystems
description: Rare and powerful compounds, known as keystone molecules, can build a web of invisible interactions among species.

title: Years After the Early Death of a Math Genius, Her Ideas Gain New Life
description: A new proof extends the work of the late Maryam Mirzakhani, cementing her legacy as a pioneer of alien mathematical realms.

title: The Physicist Working to Build Science-Literate AI
description: By training machine learning models with enough examples of basic science, Miles Cranmer hopes to push the pace of scientific discovery forward.

title: The ‘Elegant’ Math Model That Could Help Rescue Coral Reefs
description: Physicists and marine biologists built a quantitative framework that predicts how coral polyps collectively construct a variety of coral shapes.

title: New Maps of the Bizarre, Chaotic Space-Time Inside Black Holes
description: Physicists hope that understanding the churning region near singularities might help them reconcile gravity and quantum mechanics.

title: How ‘Event Scripts’ Structure Our Personal Memories
description: By screening films in a brain scanner, neuroscientists discovered a rich library of neural scripts — from a trip through an airport to a marriage proposal — that form scaffolds for memories of our experiences.

title: After 20 Years, Math Couple Solves Major Group Theory Problem
description: Britta Späth has dedicated her career to proving a single, central conjecture. She’s finally succeeded, alongside her partner, Marc Cabanes.

title: Catalytic Computing Taps the Full Power of a Full Hard Drive
description: Ten years ago, researchers proved that adding full memory can theoretically aid computation. They’re just now beginning to understand the implications.

title: The Largest Sofa You Can Move Around a Corner
description: A new proof reveals the answer to the decades-old “moving sofa” problem. It highlights how even the simplest optimization problems can have counterintuitive answers.

title: How Hans Bethe Stumbled Upon Perfect Quantum Theories
description: Quantum calculations amount to sophisticated estimates. But in 1931, Hans Bethe intuited precisely how a chain of particles would behave — an insight that had far-reaching consequences.

title: Undergraduate Upends a 40-Year-Old Data Science Conjecture
description: A young computer scientist and two colleagues show that searches within data structures called hash tables can be much faster than previously deemed possible.

title: How Noether’s Theorem Revolutionized Physics
description: Emmy Noether showed that fundamental physical laws are just a consequence of simple symmetries. A century later, her insights continue to shape physics.

title: The Poetry Fan Who Taught an LLM to Read and Write DNA
description: By treating DNA as a language, Brian Hie’s “ChatGPT for genomes” could pick up patterns that humans can’t see, accelerating biological design.

title: New Proofs Probe the Limits of Mathematical Truth
description: By proving a broader version of Hilbert’s famous 10th problem, two groups of mathematicians have expanded the realm of mathematical unknowability.

title: Chatbot Software Begins to Face Fundamental Limitations
description: Recent results show that large language models struggle with compositional tasks, suggesting a hard limit to their abilities.

title: How Does Life Happen When There’s Barely Any Light?
description: Under the sea ice during the Arctic’s pitch-black polar night, cells power photosynthesis on the lowest light levels ever observed in nature.

title: Cosmologists Try a New Way to Measure the Shape of the Universe
description: Is the universe flat and infinite, or something more complex? We can’t say for sure, but a new search strategy is mapping out the subtle signals that could reveal if the universe has a shape.

title: New Book-Sorting Algorithm Almost Reaches Perfection
description: The library sorting problem is used across computer science for organizing far more than just books. A new solution is less than a page-width away from the theoretical ideal.

title: The Jagged, Monstrous Function That Broke Calculus
description: In the late 19th century, Karl Weierstrass invented a fractal-like function that was decried as nothing less than a “deplorable evil.” In time, it would transform the foundations of mathematics.

title: Concept Cells Help Your Brain Abstract Information and Build Memories
description: Individual cells in the brain light up for specific ideas. These concept neurons, once known as “Jennifer Aniston cells,” help us think, imagine and remember episodes from our lives.

title: Heat Destroys All Order. Except for in This One Special Case.
description: Heat is supposed to ruin anything it touches. But physicists have shown that an idealized form of magnetism is heatproof.

title: Mathematicians Discover New Way for Spheres to ‘Kiss’
description: A new proof marks the first progress in decades on important cases of the so-called kissing problem. Getting there meant doing away with traditional approaches.

title: Can AI Models Show Us How People Learn? Impossible Languages Point a Way.
description: Certain grammatical rules never appear in any known language. By constructing artificial languages that have these rules, linguists can use neural networks to explore how people learn.

title: The Physicist Decoding the Nonbinary Nature of the Subatomic World
description: Inside the proton, quarks and gluons shift and morph their properties in ways that physicists are still struggling to understand. Rithya Kunnawalkam Elayavalli brings to the problem a perspective unlike many of their peers.

title: Rational or Not? This Basic Math Question Took Decades To Answer.
description: It’s surprisingly difficult to prove one of the most basic properties of a number: whether it can be written as a fraction. A broad new method can help settle this ancient question.

title: The Ocean Teems With Networks of Interconnected Bacteria
description: Nanotube bridge networks grow between the most abundant photosynthetic bacteria in the oceans, suggesting that the world is far more interconnected than anyone realized.

title: Why Computer Scientists Consult Oracles
description: Hypothetical devices that can quickly and accurately answer questions have become a powerful tool in computational complexity theory.

title: Scientists Re-Create the Microbial Dance That Sparked Complex Life
description: Evolution was fueled by endosymbiosis, cellular alliances in which one microbe makes a permanent home inside another. For the first time, biologists made it happen in the lab.

title: The Year in Computer Science
description: Researchers got a better look at the thoughts of chatbots, amateurs learned exactly how complicated simple systems can be, and quantum computers passed an essential milestone.

title: How Will We Know We’re Not Alone?
description: The first planet beyond our solar system was identified just 30 years ago. Since then, thousands have been found and characterized. As we look for more, exoplanet experts are also probing for signs of alien biospheres hundreds of light-years away. In this episode, co-host Janna Levin speaks with astrophysicist and astrobiologist Lisa Kaltenegger about how we’ll know we’re not alone in the cosmos.

title: The Year in Biology
description: Biologists used artificial intelligence to make discoveries about molecules and the brain, and overturned long-held assumptions about the immune system and RNA.

title: The Year in Physics
description: Physicists discovered strange supersolids, constructed new kinds of superconductors, and continued to make the case that the cosmos is far weirder than anyone suspected.

title: The Year in Math
description: Landmark results in geometry and number theory marked an exciting year for mathematics, at a time when advances in artificial intelligence are starting to transform the subject’s future.

title: What Is Entropy? A Measure of Just How Little We Really Know.
description: Exactly 200 years ago, a French engineer introduced an idea that would quantify the universe’s inexorable slide into decay. But entropy, as it’s currently understood, is less a fact about the world than a reflection of our growing ignorance. Embracing that truth is leading to a rethink of everything from rational decision-making to the limits of machines.

title: Mathematicians Uncover a New Way to Count Prime Numbers
description: To make progress on one of number theory’s most elementary questions, two mathematicians turned to an unlikely source.

title: Quantum Computers Cross Critical Error Threshold
description: In a first, researchers have shown that adding more “qubits” to a quantum computer can make it more resilient. It’s an essential step on the long road to practical applications.

title: Exotic New Superconductors Delight and Confound
description: Three new species of superconductivity were spotted this year, illustrating the myriad ways electrons can join together to form a frictionless quantum soup.

title: How Is Cell Death Essential to Life?
description: Cells in our bodies are constantly dying — and these countless tiny deaths are essential to human health and multicellular life itself. In this episode, co-host Steven Strogatz speaks with cellular biologist Shai Shaham about what makes a cell “alive” and the latest developments in understanding how and why cells die.

title: The AI Pioneer With Provocative Plans for Humanity
description: While some fret about technology’s social impacts, Raj Reddy still believes in the power of artificial intelligence to improve lives.

title: Fish Have a Brain Microbiome. Could Humans Have One Too?
description: The discovery that other vertebrates have healthy, microbial brains is fueling the still controversial possibility that we might have them as well.

title: Teen Mathematicians Tie Knots Through a Mind-Blowing Fractal
description: Three high schoolers and their mentor revisited a century-old theorem to prove that all knots can be found in a fractal called the Menger sponge.

title: What Is Distributed Computing?
description: Our computers can get a lot more done when they share the load with other machines.

title: In the Quantum World, Even Points of View Are Uncertain
description: The reference frames from which observers view quantum events can themselves have multiple possible locations at once — an insight with potentially major ramifications.

title: What Can Birdsong Teach Us About Human Language?
description: We often consider spoken language to be a feature that distinguishes humans from other forms of animal life. Brain research, however, suggests that other creatures — including certain birds — share some of our neural circuitry related to language. In this episode, co-host Janna Levin explores the origins and underlying mechanisms of human speech and birdsong with neurobiologist and geneticist Erich Jarvis.

title: All Life on Earth Today Descended From a Single Cell. Meet LUCA.
description: The clearest picture yet of our “last universal common ancestor” suggests it was a relatively complex organism living 4.2 billion years ago, a time long considered too harsh for life to flourish.

title: Mathematical Thinking Isn’t What You Think It Is
description: The mathematician David Bessis claims that everyone is capable of, and can benefit greatly from, mathematical thinking.

title: How Public Key Cryptography Really Works, Using Only Simple Math
description: The security system that underlies the internet makes use of a curious fact: You can broadcast part of your encryption to make your information much more secure.

title: The Cosmos Teems with Complex Organic Molecules
description: Wherever astronomers look, they see life’s raw materials.

title: New Elliptic Curve Breaks 18-Year-Old Record
description: Two mathematicians have renewed a debate about the fundamental nature of some of math’s most important equations.

title: Debate May Help AI Models Converge on Truth
description: How do we know if a large language model is lying? Letting AI systems argue with each other may help expose the truth.

title: How Is AI Changing the Science of Prediction?
description: With lots of data, a strong model and statistical thinking, scientists can make predictions about all sorts of complex phenomena. Today, this practice is evolving to harness the power of machine learning and massive datasets. In this episode, co-host Steven Strogatz speaks with statistician Emmanuel Candès about black boxes, uncertainty and the power of inductive reasoning.

title: Physicists Spot Quantum Tornadoes Twirling in a ‘Supersolid’
description: New observations of microscopic vortices confirm the existence of a paradoxical phase of matter that may also arise inside neutron stars.

title: He’s Gleaning the Design Rules of Life to Re-Create It
description: Yizhi “Patrick” Cai is coordinating a global effort to write a complete synthetic yeast genome. If he succeeds, the resulting cell will be the artificial life most closely related to humans to date.

title: Math’s ‘Bunkbed Conjecture’ Has Been Debunked
description: It was intuitive, even obvious. It was also wrong.

title: It Might Be Possible To Detect Gravitons After All
description: A new experimental proposal suggests detecting a particle of gravity is far easier than anyone imagined. Now physicists are debating what it would really prove.

title: Meet the Eukaryote, the First Cell to Get Organized
description: All modern multicellular life — all life that any of us regularly see — is made of cells with a knack for compartmentalization. Recent discoveries are revealing how the first eukaryote got its start.

title: Computer Scientists Establish the Best Way to Traverse a Graph
description: Dijkstra’s algorithm was long thought to be the most efficient way to find a graph’s best routes. Researchers have now proved that it’s “universally optimal.”

title: Why Is It So Hard to Define a Species?
description: The idea of a species is fundamental to the way that many people understand the structure of life on Earth. But ask 10 specialists how they define the concept and you might get 10 answers. In this episode, co-host Janna Levin speaks with evolutionary biologist Kevin de Queiroz about what makes defining and delineating species such a slippery process, and why it matters to our understanding of both evolution and conservation.

title: How Do Merging Supermassive Black Holes Pass the Final Parsec?
description: The giant holes in galaxies’ centers shouldn’t be able to merge, yet merge they do. Scientists suggest that an unusual form of dark matter may be the solution.

title: Math Is Still Catching Up to the Mysterious Genius of Srinivasa Ramanujan
description: Born poor in colonial India and dead at 32, Ramanujan had fantastical, out-of-nowhere visions that continue to shape the field today.

title: How the Human Brain Contends With the Strangeness of Zero
description: Zero, which was invented late in history, is special among numbers. New studies are uncovering how the brain creates something out of nothing.

title: ‘Quantum Memory’ Proves Exponentially Powerful
description: Researchers are exploring new ways that quantum computers will be able to reveal the secrets of complex quantum systems.

title: Big Advance on Simple-Sounding Math Problem Was a Century in the Making
description: A new proof about prime numbers illuminates the subtle relationship between addition and multiplication — and raises hopes for progress on the famous abc conjecture.

title: Even a Single Bacterial Cell Can Sense the Seasons Changing
description: Though they live only a few hours before dividing, bacteria can anticipate the approach of cold weather and prepare for it. The discovery suggests that seasonal tracking is fundamental to life.

title: How Can Math Help Beat Cancer?
description: Cancer treatment has come a long way in recent decades. But finding the best course of treatment for each case of this diverse, dynamic disease remains a challenge. In this episode, co-host Steven Strogatz speaks with computational biologist Franziska Michor about how math, statistical models and machine learning may be critical to the next generation of cancer care.

title: The ‘Beautiful Confusion’ of the First Billion Years Comes Into View
description: Astronomers are reveling in the James Webb Space Telescope’s discoveries about the formative epoch of cosmic history.

title: The Computer Scientist Who Builds Big Pictures From Small Details
description: To better understand machine learning algorithms, Lenka Zdeborová treats them like physical materials.

title: Computer Scientists Combine Two ‘Beautiful’ Proof Methods
description: Three researchers have figured out how to craft a proof that spreads out information while keeping it perfectly secret.

title: When Data Is Missing, Scientists Guess. Then Guess Again.
description: Across the social and biological sciences, statisticians use a technique that leverages randomness to deal with the unknown.

title: The Hidden World of Electrostatic Ecology
description: Invisibly to us, insects and other tiny creatures use static electricity to travel, avoid predators, collect pollen and more. New experiments explore how evolution may have influenced this phenomenon.

title: What Can Cave Life Tell Us About Alien Ecosystems?
description: Extremophiles, or microbes that live in the most seemingly hostile environments, are the darlings of astrobiologists, who study the potential for life beyond Earth. In this episode, co-host Janna Levin speaks with astrobiologist and cave explorer Penelope Boston about how life finds a way — and whether it might have found a way elsewhere in our solar system or around a distant star.

title: Can Space-Time Be Saved?
description: Curious connections between physics and math suggest to Latham Boyle that space-time may survive the jump to the next theory of reality.

title: Physicists Reveal a Quantum Geometry That Exists Outside of Space and Time
description: A decade after the discovery of the “amplituhedron,” physicists have excavated more of the timeless geometry underlying the standard picture of how particles move.

title: If the Universe Is a Hologram, This Long-Forgotten Math Could Decode It
description: A 1930s-era breakthrough is helping physicists understand how quantum threads could weave together into a holographic space-time fabric.

title: The #1 Clue to Quantum Gravity Sits on the Surfaces of Black Holes
description: A black hole formula worked out in the 1970s remains the most concrete clue physicists have about the threads of the space-time fabric.

title: The Two Faces of Space-Time
description: A mysterious phenomenon known as duality often leads to new discoveries in physics. This time, space-time itself can sometimes be two things at once.

title: The Logic That Must Lie Behind a New Physics
description: The philosopher Karen Crowther digs into how the space-time fabric could possibly emerge from something non-spatiotemporal.

title: The Thought Experiments That Fray the Fabric of Space-Time
description: These three imagined scenarios lead many physicists to doubt that space-time is fundamental.

title: John Wheeler Saw the Tear in Reality
description: Until his dying days, the giant of 20th-century physics obsessed over the underpinnings of space and time, and how we can all share the same version of them.

title: The Unraveling of Space-Time
description: This special issue of Quanta Magazine explores the ultimate scientific quest: the search for the fundamental nature of reality.

title: Mathematicians Discover New Shapes to Solve Decades-Old Geometry Problem
description: Mathematicians have long wondered how “shapes of constant width” behave in higher dimensions. A surprisingly simple construction has given them an answer.

title: How ‘Embeddings’ Encode What Words Mean — Sort Of
description: Machines work with words by embedding their relationships with other words in a string of numbers.

title: Cells Across the Tree of Life Exchange ‘Text Messages’ Using RNA
description: Cells across the tree of life can swap short-lived messages encoded by RNA — missives that resemble a quick text rather than a formal memo on letterhead.

title: The Search for What Shook the Earth for Nine Days Straight
description: Last year, an immense but brief outburst of seismic energy was soon followed by a long hum that made the world ring. Finding its cause took 68 scientists and an assist by the Danish military.

title: Can Thermodynamics Go Quantum?
description: The Industrial Revolution brought us the laws of thermodynamics, and new ideas about work, energy and efficiency. In this episode, co-host Steven Strogatz speaks with theoretical physicist Nicole Yunger Halpern about what these concepts might mean in the age of quantum mechanics.

title: Novel Architecture Makes Neural Networks More Understandable
description: By tapping into a decades-old mathematical principle, researchers are hoping that Kolmogorov-Arnold networks will facilitate scientific discovery.

title: The Cellular Secret to Resisting the Pressure of the Deep Sea
description: Cell membranes from comb jellies reveal a new kind of adaptation to the deep sea: curvy lipids that conform to an ideal shape under pressure.

title: ‘Groups’ Underpin Modern Math. Here’s How They Work.
description: What do the integers have in common with the symmetries of a triangle? In the 19th century, mathematicians invented groups as an answer to this question.

title: The First Nuclear Clock Will Test if Fundamental Constants Change
description: An ultra-precise measurement of a transition in the hearts of thorium atoms gives physicists a tool to probe the forces that bind the universe.

title: How the Higgs Field (Actually) Gives Mass to Elementary Particles
description: In this article adapted from his new book, "Waves in an Impossible Sea," physicist Matt Strassler explains that the origin of mass in the universe has a lot to do with music.

title: Perplexing the Web, One Probability Puzzle at a Time
description: The mathematician Daniel Litt has driven social media users to distraction with a series of simple-seeming but counterintuitive probability puzzles.

title: Do We Need a New Theory of Gravity?
description: Since Newton had his initial revelation about gravity, our understanding of this fundamental concept has evolved in unexpected ways. In this week’s episode, theoretical physicist Claudia de Rham and co-host Janna Levin discuss the ways our current understanding of gravity needs to continue to evolve.

title: Computer Scientists Prove That Heat Destroys Quantum Entanglement
description: While devising a new quantum algorithm, four researchers accidentally established a hard limit on entanglement.

title: How Our Longest Nerve Orchestrates the Mind-Body Connection
description: Like a highway system, the vagus nerve branches profusely from your brain through your organs to marshal bodily functions, including aspects of mind such as mood, pleasure and fear.

title: How Colorful Ribbon Diagrams Became the Face of Proteins
description: Proteins are often visualized as cascades of curled ribbons and twisted strings, which both reveal and conceal the mess of atoms that make up these impossibly complex molecules.

title: Mathematicians Prove Hawking Wrong About the Most Extreme Black Holes
description: For decades, extremal black holes were considered mathematically impossible. A new proof reveals otherwise.

title: Diminishing Dark Energy May Evade the ‘Swampland’ of Impossible Universes
description: The largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos hints that the dark energy that’s fueling the universe’s expansion may be weakening. One community of theoretical physicists expected as much.

title: The Viral Paleontologist Who Unearths Pathogens’ Deep Histories
description: Sébastien Calvignac-Spencer searches museum jars for genetic traces of flu, measles and other viruses. Their evolutionary stories can help treat modern outbreaks and prepare for future ones.

title: Are Robots About to Level Up?
description: Today’s AI largely lives in computers, but acting and reacting in the real world — that’s the realm of robots. In this week’s episode, co-host Steven Strogatz talks with pioneering roboticist Daniela Rus about creativity, collaboration, and the unusual forms robots of the future might take.

title: The Webb Telescope Further Deepens the Biggest Controversy in Cosmology
description: A long-awaited study of the cosmic expansion rate suggests that when it comes to the Hubble tension, cosmologists are still missing something.

title: The Geometric Tool That Solved Einstein’s Relativity Problem
description: Tensors are used all over math and science to reveal hidden geometric truths. What are they?

title: How Base 3 Computing Beats Binary
description: Long explored but infrequently embraced, base 3 computing may yet find a home in cybersecurity.

title: Physicists Pinpoint the Quantum Origin of the Greenhouse Effect
description: Carbon dioxide’s powerful heat-trapping effect has been traced to a quirk of its quantum structure. The finding may explain climate change better than any computer model.

title: Grad Students Find Inevitable Patterns in Big Sets of Numbers
description: A new proof marks the first progress in decades on a problem about how order emerges from disorder.

title: What Is Analog Computing?
description: You don’t need 0s and 1s to perform computations, and in some cases it’s better to avoid them.

title: What Happens in a Mind That Can’t ‘See’ Mental Images
description: Neuroscience research into people with aphantasia, who don’t experience mental imagery, is revealing how imagination works and demonstrating the sweeping variety in our subjective experiences.

title: How Does Math Keep Secrets?
description: Cryptography is the thread that connects Julius Caesar, World War II and quantum computing, and it now lies under nearly every part of modern life. In this week’s episode, computer scientist Boaz Barak and co-host Janna Levin discuss the past and future of secrecy.

title: ‘Metaphysical Experiments’ Probe Our Hidden Assumptions About Reality
description: Experiments that test physics and philosophy "as a single whole" may be our only route to surefire knowledge about the universe.

title: With ‘Digital Twins,’ The Doctor Will See You Now
description: By creating digital twins of patients, Amanda Randles wants to bring unprecedented precision to medical forecasts.

title: The Physics of Cold Water May Have Jump-Started Complex Life
